summary.headline: Inflation just won't quit
summary.tldr: Inflation remains stubbornly high, with both headline and core inflation above expectations in October. Experts suggest this is due to broader price pressures, not just energy costs. The Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates again in December.

key_points.point: Inflation remains high, with headline inflation rising 0.4% in October and core inflation rising 0.3%, both above expectations.
key_points.why_it_matters: These figures indicate that inflation is not slowing down as quickly as some had hoped.

key_points.point: Gasoline prices rose 1% in October, contributing to headline inflation.
key_points.why_it_matters: Higher energy prices are still a factor, but inflation is also spreading to other areas of the economy.

key_points.point: Inflation is no longer limited to energy and food; it is now affecting services like vehicle insurance, hospital services, and streaming platforms.
key_points.why_it_matters: This suggests that inflation is becoming more widespread and harder to control.

key_points.point: High energy prices are now bleeding into other parts of the economy, including services not directly affected by oil prices.
key_points.why_it_matters: This indicates that inflation is becoming more generalized and may be harder to reduce.

key_points.point: Tight labor markets and strong demand from businesses and consumers are contributing to sustained inflation.
key_points.why_it_matters: These factors give businesses more pricing power, which can keep inflation elevated.

key_points.point: Housing costs are rising due to high mortgage rates and a shortage of homes for sale, pushing more people into rentals.
key_points.why_it_matters: This adds to the overall cost of living and can contribute to higher inflation.

summary.lesson: Inflation is still a major concern, with prices rising across the economy. The Federal Reserve is likely to take action to address this, and consumers are feeling the pressure. Understanding inflation and its causes is important for making informed financial decisions.
opinions_and_predictions: Andrew Davis at Bryn Mawr Trust says there's almost nothing going in the right direction with inflation.
Thomas Ryan at Capital Economics calls the CPI release a 'shocker.'
Brian Bethune at Boston College says inflation pressures are becoming broader than energy.
Andrew Davis says businesses are able to push through higher prices.
Bethann Bovino at U.S. Bank says the typical consumer is falling behind with every paycheck.
Gregory Brew with Eurasia Group says the oil market is finding ways to get closer to normal, bringing prices down.
Tom Kloza with Gulf Oil says diesel prices are ticking down, but a meaningful and sustained drop could be a while.
Debnel Chowdhury with S&P Global Energy says we don't expect the damage to be repaired in a meaningful way until next year.
Jean Chatzky says retirees are often scared to spend their savings, which has a significant impact on the economy.

glossary.definition: Consumer Price Index, a measure of inflation that tracks the average change in prices over time for a basket of goods and services commonly purchased by households. (CPI is used to measure inflation.)
A measure of inflation that excludes volatile items like food and energy. (Core inflation is used to get a better picture of long-term inflation trends.)
The overall rate of inflation, including all items in the CPI basket. (Headline inflation includes all goods and services.)
glossary.example: Headline inflation was up 0.4% in October.

glossary.definition: The cost of borrowing money, shown as a yearly percentage. The Federal Reserve sets a target for one key short-term rate (the federal funds rate), which influences, but does not directly set, rates on loans, mortgages and savings.
glossary.example: The Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates again in December.

glossary.definition: A general increase in prices over time, reducing the purchasing power of money. (Inflation makes things more expensive.)
A regular payment made to a person after they retire, typically from an employer or government. (Pensions provide income in retirement.)
glossary.example: Pension checks came in every month until the person died.
